data.title: Rapamycin alleviates toxicity of different aggregate-prone proteins
data.authors: Berger Z; Ravikumar B; Menzies FM; Oroz LG; Underwood BR; Pangalos MN; Schmitt I; Wullner U; Evert BO; O'Kane CJ; Rubinsztein DC

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Mammalian cell lines (incl. COS cells) expressing polyglutamine- and polyalanine-expanded proteins; Drosophila expressing wild-type or mutant human tau
data.finding: Building on their earlier work with mutant huntingtin, the authors showed in cell models that rapamycin, used as an autophagy inducer, increased the clearance of several proteins with long polyglutamine tracts and of a polyalanine-expanded protein, and reduced their toxicity. In fruit flies expressing wild-type or mutant human tau, rapamycin reduced tau toxicity, and this went with less insoluble tau. The authors argued that inducing autophagy with rapamycin could be useful across several aggregate-prone protein diseases, not only Huntington's disease. Boundary: cultured cells and Drosophila overexpressing disease proteins; drawn from the abstract only; no mammalian in vivo or human data.
data.abstract_excerpt: Many neurodegenerative diseases are caused by intracellular, aggregate-prone proteins, including polyglutamine-expanded huntingtin in Huntington's disease (HD) and mutant tau in fronto-temporal dementia/tauopathy. Previously, we showed that rapamycin, an autophagy inducer, enhances mutant huntingtin fragment clearance and attenuated toxicity. Here we show much wider applications for this approach. Rapamycin enhances the autophagic clearance of different proteins with long polyglutamines and a polyalanine-expanded protein, and reduces their toxicity.

extracted_findings.effect: Rapamycin increased autophagic clearance and reduced toxicity of polyQ/polyA proteins and tau
